name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q01 - Acceleration due to gravity on non-uniform earth

questiontext.text: 8.1 The earth is an approximate sphere. If the interior contained matter which is not of the same density everywhere, then on the surface of the earth, the acceleration due to gravity

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
By Newton's law of universal gravitation, every mass element inside the earth attracts a test mass on the surface toward itself. The net gravitational field \(\mathbf{g}\) at any point on the surface is the vector sum of the contributions from all mass elements in the earth's interior.

Step 2: Evaluation
If the density inside the earth is not uniform everywhere (for example, asymmetric mass distribution), the magnitude of \(\mathbf{g}\) will vary from place to place and its direction need not point strictly toward the geometric centre of the sphere. However, at any point on the outer surface of the earth, all the matter of the earth lies on one side of the tangent plane passing through that point. Consequently, every mass element produces a gravitational force component along the inward normal to the surface.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because all inward normal components add up constructively and are strictly positive, the net acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the earth cannot be zero at any point.

answer.text: will be directed towards the centre but not the same everywhere.
will have the same value everywhere but not directed towards the centre.
will be same everywhere in magnitude directed towards the centre.
cannot be zero at any point.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q02 - Apparent motion of Mercury observed from Earth

questiontext.text: 8.2 As observed from earth, the sun appears to move in an approximate circular orbit. For the motion of another planet like mercury as observed from earth, this would

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Newton's law of gravitation, the gravitational force between two bodies is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. In the solar system, the sun's mass is overwhelmingly larger than that of any planet.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because the sun is much more massive than the earth, the dominant gravitational force acting on Mercury is due to the sun, not the earth. Therefore, Mercury revolves around the sun rather than around the earth. As observed from the earth—which is itself revolving around the sun—the relative motion of Mercury appears complex (including apparent retrograde loops) rather than an approximate circular orbit around the earth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The statement is not true for Mercury as observed from earth because the major gravitational force on Mercury is due to the sun.

answer.text: be similarly true.
not be true because the force between earth and mercury is not inverse square law.
not be true because the major gravitational force on mercury is due to sun.
not be true because mercury is influenced by forces other than gravitational forces.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q03 - Net gravitational torque on uniform spherical earth

questiontext.text: 8.3 Different points in earth are at slightly different distances from the sun and hence experience different forces due to gravitation. For a rigid body, we know that if various forces act at various points in it, the resultant motion is as if a net force acts on the c.m. (centre of mass) causing translation and a net torque at the c.m. causing rotation around an axis through the c.m. For the earth-sun system (approximating the earth as a uniform density sphere)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For a spherically symmetric body of uniform density, the gravitational interaction with an external point mass (or spherically symmetric sun) is equivalent to having the entire mass of the sphere concentrated at its centre of mass. The torque \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) about the centre of mass is given by \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\), where \(\mathbf{r}\) is the position vector of the point of application of the effective force relative to the centre of mass.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because the earth is approximated as a uniform density sphere, the resultant gravitational force exerted by the sun passes directly through the centre of mass of the earth. Thus, the position vector \(\mathbf{r}\) from the centre of mass to the line of action of the resultant force is zero (or the angle between \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{F}\) is zero for all symmetric pairs of mass elements).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the net gravitational torque acting on the earth about its centre of mass due to the sun is zero.

answer.text: the torque is zero.
the torque causes the earth to spin.
the rigid body result is not applicable since the earth is not even approximately a rigid body.
the torque causes the earth to move around the sun.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q04 - Finite life and decay of orbiting satellites

questiontext.text: 8.4 Satellites orbiting the earth have finite life and sometimes debris of satellites fall to the earth. This is because,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A satellite in a low-earth orbit moves through the tenuous upper layers of the earth's atmosphere. The total mechanical energy of a satellite of mass \(m\) in a circular orbit of radius \(r\) around the earth of mass \(M\) is \(E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
As the satellite moves through the upper atmosphere, it experiences viscous drag (atmospheric friction). This dissipative force does negative work on the satellite, continuously reducing its total mechanical energy \(E\) (making it more negative). Consequently, the orbital radius \(r\)—and hence the height of the satellite above the earth—gradually decreases until the satellite spirals inward and falls toward the earth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Satellites have a finite lifetime and eventually fall to the earth because of viscous forces causing the speed and height of the satellite to gradually decrease.

answer.text: the solar cells and batteries in satellites run out.
the laws of gravitation predict a trajectory spiralling inwards.
of viscous forces causing the speed of satellite and hence height to gradually decrease.
of collisions with other satellites.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q05 - Orbit of the moon observed from sun

questiontext.text: 8.5 Both earth and moon are subject to the gravitational force of the sun. As observed from the sun, the orbit of the moon

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Kepler's first law, a body moves in a strictly elliptical orbit around a fixed centre only when the net force acting on it is a central force directed toward that fixed centre and varying inversely as the square of the distance.

Step 2: Evaluation
The moon is subject to two major gravitational forces: one toward the sun and another toward the earth. Since the moon is not generally on the line joining the sun and the earth, the resultant gravitational force on the moon does not always point toward the sun. Hence, the total gravitational force on the moon as observed from the sun is not central.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because the total gravitational force acting on the moon is not central with respect to the sun, the orbit of the moon as observed from the sun will not be strictly elliptical.

answer.text: will be elliptical.
will not be strictly elliptical because the total gravitational force on it is not central.
is not elliptical but will necessarily be a closed curve.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q06 - Motion of asteroids around the sun

questiontext.text: 8.6 In our solar system, the inter-planetary region has chunks of matter (much smaller in size compared to planets) called asteroids. They

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Under Newton's law of gravitation, the acceleration of any body orbiting the sun is \(\mathbf{a} = -\frac{GM_{\text{s}}}{r^2}\hat{\mathbf{r}}\), which is independent of the mass of the orbiting body. Kepler's laws apply to any object moving under an inverse-square central gravitational force.

Step 2: Evaluation
Even though asteroids have much smaller masses than planets, they experience the same inverse-square central gravitational force from the sun. Their orbital motion is governed by the same equations of motion as planets.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Asteroids will move in orbits around the sun just like planets and will obey Kepler's laws.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q07 - Properties of inertial and gravitational mass

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Inertial mass \(m_i\) measures a body's resistance to acceleration under an external force (\(F = m_i a\)), while gravitational mass \(m_g\) determines the gravitational force experienced by the body in a gravitational field (\(F_g = m_g g\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
Experimental observations (such as the Eötvös experiment) confirm that gravitational mass and inertial mass are equal for all bodies, which is why the acceleration due to gravity \(g = \frac{m_g}{m_i} \frac{GM}{R^2}\) is the same for all objects on earth. Both inertial mass and gravitational mass are intrinsic properties of a particle and do not depend on the presence of neighbouring heavy objects.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The statement that the gravitational mass of a particle like a proton can depend on the presence of neighbouring heavy objects while the inertial mass cannot is false, making it the wrong option.

answer.text: Inertial mass is a measure of difficulty of accelerating a body by an external force whereas the gravitational mass is relevant in determining the gravitational force on it by an external mass.
That the gravitational mass and inertial mass are equal is an experimental result.
That the acceleration due to gravity on earth is the same for all bodies is due to the equality of gravitational mass and inertial mass.
Gravitational mass of a particle like proton can depend on the presence of neighbouring heavy objects but the inertial mass cannot.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q08 - Motion of particle between two unequal masses

questiontext.text:
8.8 Particles of masses \(2M\), \(m\) and \(M\) are respectively at points \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) with \(AB = \frac{1}{2}(BC)\). \(m\) is much-much smaller than \(M\) and at time \(t = 0\), they are all at rest (Fig. 8.1).

At subsequent times before any collision takes place:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Three particles of masses \(m_A = 2M\), \(m_B = m\), and \(m_C = M\) are collinear at points \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\), with \(B\) lying between \(A\) and \(C\). The distances satisfy \(AB = \frac{1}{2}(BC)\). Also, \(m \ll M\), and all particles are initially at rest at \(t = 0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let \(AB = x\), so \(BC = 2x\). Take the direction from \(B\) toward \(A\) (toward \(2M\)) as positive along the line \(AC\). Since \(m \ll M\), the motion of the heavy masses \(2M\) and \(M\) toward each other is initially negligible compared to the acceleration of \(m\), or we compare the gravitational forces acting directly on \(m\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the gravitational force between two masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) separated by distance \(r\) is:
\[F = \frac{Gm_1 m_2}{r^2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The gravitational force on mass \(m\) at \(B\) due to mass \(2M\) at \(A\) is directed toward \(A\) and has magnitude:
\[F_{BA} = \frac{G(2M)m}{x^2} = \frac{2GMm}{x^2}\]
The gravitational force on mass \(m\) at \(B\) due to mass \(M\) at \(C\) is directed toward \(C\) and has magnitude:
\[F_{BC} = \frac{GMm}{(2x)^2} = \frac{GMm}{4x^2}\]
Comparing the two magnitudes:
\[F_{BA} - F_{BC} = \frac{2GMm}{x^2} - \frac{GMm}{4x^2} = \frac{7GMm}{4x^2} > 0\]
Since \(F_{BA} > F_{BC}\), the net force on \(m\) is directed toward \(2M\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because \(m\) starts from rest and experiences a net force toward \(2M\), and as it moves closer to \(2M\) the force \(F_{BA}\) increases while \(F_{BC}\) decreases, \(m\) will continue to move towards \(2M\).

answer.text: \(m\) will remain at rest.
\(m\) will move towards \(M\).
\(m\) will move towards \(2M\).
\(m\) will have oscillatory motion.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q09 - Variation of acceleration due to gravity

questiontext.text: 8.9 Which of the following options are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The acceleration due to gravity on the surface of a uniform spherical earth of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) is \(g = \frac{GM}{R^2}\). Its value varies with altitude \(h\), depth \(d\), and latitude \(\lambda\).

Step 2: Evaluation
1. With increasing altitude \(h\), the acceleration due to gravity is \(g_h = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2} = \frac{g}{(1+h/R)^2}\), which clearly decreases as \(h\) increases.
2. With increasing depth \(d\) inside a uniform-density earth, \(g_d = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)\), which decreases (not increases) as \(d\) increases.
3. Due to the rotation of the earth with angular speed \(\omega\), the effective acceleration due to gravity at latitude \(\lambda\) is \(g_\lambda = g - \omega^2 R \cos^2\lambda\). As latitude \(\lambda\) increases from \(0^\circ\) (equator) to \(90^\circ\) (poles), \(\cos\lambda\) decreases from \(1\) to \(0\), so \(g_\lambda\) increases.
4. Since \(g = \frac{GM}{R^2}\), \(g\) is directly proportional to the mass \(M\) of the earth and is not independent of it.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, acceleration due to gravity decreases with increasing altitude and increases with increasing latitude.

answer.text: Acceleration due to gravity decreases with increasing altitude.
Acceleration due to gravity increases with increasing depth (assume the earth to be a sphere of uniform density).
Acceleration due to gravity increases with increasing latitude.
Acceleration due to gravity is independent of the mass of the earth.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q10 - Consequences of an inverse-cube gravitational law

questiontext.text: 8.10 If the law of gravitation, instead of being inverse-square law, becomes an inverse-cube law-

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Suppose the gravitational force between two masses \(M\) and \(m\) separated by distance \(r\) follows an inverse-cube law instead of an inverse-square law, i.e., \(F = \frac{GMm}{r^3}\) (with \(G\) having suitably modified dimensions).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
We consider a planet of mass \(m\) orbiting a sun of mass \(M\) (\(M \gg m\)), a stone thrown near the surface of the earth (radius \(R\), height \(h \ll R\)), and a point mass inside a uniform spherical shell.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a circular orbit of radius \(r\), the centripetal force is provided by the gravitational force: \(\frac{mv^2}{r} = F(r)\). Closed elliptical orbits for general bound initial conditions require an inverse-square central force (or Hooke's law force). Near the earth's surface, \(r = R + h \approx R\), so \(g'\) is nearly constant.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Since the force is \(F \propto \frac{1}{r^3}\) rather than \(\frac{1}{r^2}\), bound non-circular orbits are spirals (Cotes' spirals) and planets will not have elliptic orbits.
2. For a circular orbit, \(\frac{GMm}{r^3} = \frac{mv^2}{r} \implies v = \frac{\sqrt{GM}}{r}\). Thus, a circular orbit is still mathematically possible at this speed.
3. Near the surface of the earth, \(g' = \frac{GM_E}{(R+h)^3} \approx \frac{GM_E}{R^3}\) is approximately constant for \(h \ll R\). Under a nearly constant downward acceleration, the trajectory of a stone thrown by hand is approximately parabolic.
4. Newton's shell theorem (zero force inside a uniform spherical shell) holds strictly only for an inverse-square force law; for an inverse-cube law, the gravitational force inside a spherical shell of uniform density is generally non-zero.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Hence, under an inverse-cube law of gravitation, planets will not have elliptic orbits, and the projectile motion of a stone thrown by hand on the surface of the earth will be approximately parabolic.

answer.text: planets will not have elliptic orbits.
circular orbits of planets is not possible.
projectile motion of a stone thrown by hand on the surface of the earth will be approximately parabolic.
there will be no gravitational force inside a spherical shell of uniform density.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q11 - Effects of changing G and sun's mass

questiontext.text: 8.11 If the mass of sun were ten times smaller and gravitational constant \(G\) were ten times larger in magnitudes-

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The new mass of the sun is \(M_s' = \frac{M_s}{10}\) and the new universal gravitational constant is \(G' = 10G\). The mass of the earth \(M_E\) and its radius \(R_E\) remain unchanged.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
We evaluate the effects on the acceleration due to gravity \(g'\) at the earth's surface, the weight of objects, the terminal velocity of raindrops, and the lift required for airplanes.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Acceleration due to gravity on earth: \(g = \frac{GM_E}{R_E^2}\).
Terminal velocity of a spherical raindrop of radius \(r\) and density \(\rho\) in air of viscosity \(\eta\): \(v_T = \frac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta} \propto g\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The new acceleration due to gravity on the earth's surface becomes:
\[g' = \frac{G' M_E}{R_E^2} = \frac{10G M_E}{R_E^2} = 10g\]
1. Since \(g' = 10g\), the acceleration due to gravity on earth changes by a factor of \(10\).
2. A person's weight becomes \(W' = mg' = 10mg\), making walking on the ground much more difficult.
3. Since terminal velocity \(v_T \propto g'\), raindrops will fall ten times faster (much faster).
4. To generate enough aerodynamic lift to balance the tenfold increase in weight \(mg'\), airplanes will have to travel much faster.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, walking on ground would become more difficult, raindrops will fall much faster, and airplanes will have to travel much faster.

answer.text: walking on ground would become more difficult.
the acceleration due to gravity on earth will not change.
raindrops will fall much faster.
airplanes will have to travel much faster.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q12 - Kepler's laws with opposite charges on sun and planets

questiontext.text: 8.12 If the sun and the planets carried huge amounts of opposite charges,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kepler's three laws of planetary motion are a direct consequence of the gravitational force being an attractive, central force that obeys the inverse-square law (\(F \propto \frac{1}{r^2}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
If the sun and the planets carried huge amounts of opposite charges, an attractive electrostatic force \(F_e = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}\) would act along the line joining their centres in addition to the attractive gravitational force \(F_g = \frac{GMm}{r^2}\). Both forces are radial (central) and follow the inverse-square law. Their sum \(F_{\text{net}} = F_g + F_e\) is also a central, attractive, inverse-square force. Therefore, the orbit remains an ellipse with the sun at one focus (first law), areal velocity remains constant (second law), and \(T^2 \propto a^3\) remains valid for a given planet (third law).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Consequently, all three of Kepler's laws would still be valid, the second law will not change, and the first law will still be valid.

answer.text: all three of Kepler's laws would still be valid.
only the third law will be valid.
the second law will not change.
the first law will still be valid.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q13 - Effect of decreasing gravitational constant over billions of years

questiontext.text: 8.13 There have been suggestions that the value of the gravitational constant \(G\) becomes smaller when considered over very large time period (in billions of years) in the future. If that happens, for our earth,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For the earth orbiting the sun, the gravitational attraction \(F = \frac{GM_s M_E}{r^2}\) provides the necessary centripetal force. Angular momentum \(L = M_E v r\) is conserved because the force remains central.

Step 2: Evaluation
If \(G\) gradually decreases over billions of years, the inward gravitational pull weakens. With angular momentum \(L\) conserved, the orbital radius \(r\) slowly increases over time (\(r \propto \frac{1}{G}\) for adiabatic variation). Because the radius continuously increases, the earth's path is an outward spiral rather than a strictly closed orbit. As the distance from the sun increases, the earth receives less solar radiation and becomes colder, not hotter. After a sufficiently long time as \(G\) becomes vanishingly small, the earth will no longer remain bound and will leave the solar system.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, we will be going around but not strictly in closed orbits, and after a sufficiently long time we will leave the solar system.

answer.text: nothing will change.
we will become hotter after billions of years.
we will be going around but not strictly in closed orbits.
after sufficiently long time we will leave the solar system.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q14 - Modified gravitational force law with power n

questiontext.text:
8.14 Supposing Newton's law of gravitation for gravitation forces \(\mathbf{F}_1\) and \(\mathbf{F}_2\) between two masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) at positions \(\mathbf{r}_1\) and \(\mathbf{r}_2\) read

\(\mathbf{F}_1 = -\mathbf{F}_2 = -\frac{\mathbf{r}_{12}}{r_{12}^3} G M_0^2 \left( \frac{m_1 m_2}{M_0^2} \right)^n\) where \(M_0\) is a constant of dimension of mass, \(\mathbf{r}_{12} = \mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2\) and \(n\) is a number. In such a case,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The modified gravitational force between two masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) is:
\[\mathbf{F}_1 = -\mathbf{F}_2 = -\frac{\mathbf{r}_{12}}{r_{12}^3} G M_0^2 \left(\frac{m_1 m_2}{M_0^2}\right)^n\]
where \(\mathbf{r}_{12} = \mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2\), \(M_0\) is a constant with dimensions of mass, and \(n\) is a real number.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
For an object of mass \(m\) near the surface of the earth (mass \(M_E\), radius \(R_E\)), the acceleration due to gravity is \(g = \frac{|\mathbf{F}|}{m}\). For a planet of mass \(m\) orbiting the sun of mass \(M_s\), the orbit is governed by the central force \(\mathbf{F}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = \frac{F}{m}\).
2. Kepler's laws: First and second laws require a central inverse-square force; the third law requires \(\frac{T^2}{a^3}\) to be the same constant for all planets.
3. Archimedes' principle: An object floats or sinks depending on whether its weight \(W = mg\) is less than or greater than the weight of the displaced water \(W_w = m_w g_w\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. For an object of mass \(m\) on the earth's surface:
\[g(m) = \frac{1}{m} \frac{G M_0^2}{R_E^2} \left(\frac{M_E m}{M_0^2}\right)^n = \frac{G M_0^{2-2n} M_E^n}{R_E^2} m^{n-1}\]
Unless \(n = 1\), \(g\) depends on \(m\), so the acceleration due to gravity on earth will be different for different objects.
2. Since the force is still central and inversely proportional to \(r_{12}^2\), Kepler's first law (elliptical orbits) and second law (conservation of angular momentum / equal areas in equal times) remain valid. However, the orbital period satisfies \(T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2 r^3}{g_{\text{sun}}(m) r^2} \propto m^{1-n} r^3\), so the ratio \(\frac{T^2}{r^3}\) depends on the planet's mass \(m\). Thus, only Kepler's third law becomes invalid as a universal relation across different planets.
3. Consider an object lighter than water of the same volume, so \(m_o < m_w\). Its weight is \(W_o = m_o g(m_o) \propto m_o^n\), while the buoyant force (weight of displaced water) is \(W_w = m_w g(m_w) \propto m_w^n\). If \(n < 0\), then \(m_o < m_w \implies m_o^n > m_w^n\), so \(W_o > W_w\). Hence, the object lighter than water will sink in water.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, the acceleration due to gravity on earth will be different for different objects, only the third law of Kepler will become invalid, and for \(n\) negative, an object lighter than water will sink in water.

answer.text: the acceleration due to gravity on earth will be different for different objects.
none of the three laws of Kepler will be valid.
only the third law will become invalid.
for \(n\) negative, an object lighter than water will sink in water.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q15 - Orbital directions of polar and geostationary satellites

questiontext.text: 8.15 Which of the following are true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Polar satellites and geostationary satellites have distinct orbital planes and directions of revolution around the earth.

Step 2: Evaluation
1. A polar satellite orbits in a plane passing over the earth's north and south poles, moving in the north-south direction.
2. A geostationary satellite orbits in the equatorial plane with the same angular velocity and sense of rotation as the earth about its axis. Since the earth rotates from west to east, a geostationary satellite also revolves around the earth in the west-east direction.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, a polar satellite goes around the earth's pole in the north-south direction, and a geostationary satellite goes around the earth in the west-east direction.

answer.text: A polar satellite goes around the earth's pole in north-south direction.
A geostationary satellite goes around the earth in east-west direction.
A geostationary satellite goes around the earth in west-east direction.
A polar satellite goes around the earth in east-west direction.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q16 - Centre of mass and centre of gravity

questiontext.text: 8.16 The centre of mass of an extended body on the surface of the earth and its centre of gravity

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The centre of mass (COM) of a body depends only on its mass distribution (\(\mathbf{r}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\int \mathbf{r}\,dm}{\int dm}\)) and is independent of the external gravitational field. The centre of gravity (COG) is the point where the resultant gravitational force acts (producing zero net gravitational torque), given by \(\mathbf{r}_{\text{cg}} = \frac{\int \mathbf{r}\,g(\mathbf{r})\,dm}{\int g(\mathbf{r})\,dm}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
1. In a uniform gravitational field (\(g = \text{constant}\)), the COG coincides with the COM. However, the earth's gravitational field varies with height and direction for very large bodies (such as mountains), so the COM and COG are not always at the same point for any size, even for large spherical bodies (where the lower half experiences slightly stronger gravity than the upper half).
2. For symmetric bodies in a uniform field or bodies like a horizontal uniform ring, they can coincide, so it is false to say they can never be at the same point.
3. For objects of sizes less than \(100\text{ m}\) (much smaller than the earth's radius \(R_E \approx 6.4 \times 10^6\text{ m}\)), the variation of \(g\) across the object is negligible, so the COM and COG are very close to each other.
4. If the object is taken deep inside the earth, its COG may shift due to the changing gravitational field, but its COM remains unchanged because mass distribution is an intrinsic property.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the centre of mass and the centre of gravity are close to each other for objects of sizes less than \(100\text{ m}\).

answer.text: are always at the same point for any size of the body.
are always at the same point only for spherical bodies.
can never be at the same point.
is close to each other for objects, say of sizes less than 100 m.
both can change if the object is taken deep inside the earth.
